utterances.text: Would it be right to say that the minister had authority to establish separate and special police units, operational groups, and other units?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: He also set out tasks, dead-lines for their execution of powers, and rights and obligations of the members of all -- of other units?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would it be right to say that Article 9 of these rules says that: "The department, in accordance with the plans, should conduct preparations in the case of imminent threat of war and in war should report to the -- to the bodies of the republic and cooperate with other bodies"?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Is this the basis for the decision taken in February 1999?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that these were the -- this was the approach that was also to be found in the former Law on All People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Article 10 says: "The chief of a department may establish permanent and/or ad hoc staffs, task forces, and other working groups made up of Ministry employees within the department and if so required carry out certain more complex assignments. The composition task dead-lines and other conditions as for paragraph 1 will be defined by the head of the department or the secretariat, of which the minister is to be informed immediately; is that correct.

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you know that before the minister adopted the decision dated June 16th, 1998, or May 31st, 1999, respectively, that the heads of departments passed decisions about the establishment of staffs in the territory of KiM?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: I cannot remember directly, but most probably some of the work was carried out by the heads of departments; but the heads of the secretariats also carried out such tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the minister, in June 1998 or in May 1999, took such decisions because in the staff he combined both departments and only he was authorised to give instructions to both departments and the heads of those reported exclusively to him?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I ask for two minutes to step outside if the court could pause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sure Mr. Djurdjic would not mind waiting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I would like to tender these -- this set of rules into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The rules of the Law on State Administration, is that correct, or rules on the internal organisation of the Ministry of the Interior? I believe it's a 48-page document; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. I can tell you exactly -- it is 45 pages long in the Serbian version and the English version --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are we going to need any more of it than you have dealt with in cross-examination, Mr. Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this exhibit is translated into English in its entirety. It was done in the Milutinovic et al trial, so there is a translation already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm not questioning that. We have a translation. My concern is whether we need to have 48 pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we don't need them. I would only like to tender those articles that I -- that I referred to when hearing the witness -- into evidence. I'm speaking about Article 1; Article 2; Article 3, item 2; Article 7; Article 9; Article 10; and -- and that would be all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What I think we will do, Mr. Djurdjic, is note your motion to admit perhaps Articles 1 to 10; we will hear Mr. Stamp's re-examination in case he needs to refer to any other provisions, and then we'll receive the articles that appear relevant to the case. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, am I right in saying that the minister adopted a decision on the establishment of separate police units on August the 1st, 1993?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: Most probably. I don't remember, but most likely.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right in saying that the tasks and duties of the separate police units under the decision of the minister were to preserve law and order at public gatherings, the carrying out of measures of regular and special security, and the establishment of law and order if it is seriously infringed upon, then the -- acting against rebel groups and other groups that threaten the security of the republic and the public order?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, that was the use of the units in case of need.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This could be active only upon the order of the minister?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right in saying that the police departments in the SUPs and the police administration of the ministry carried out logistical activities, administrative and technical activities, financial activities, and other activities for these units to be ready to carry out their tasks?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Let me return to something else about these units, namely, the members of these units that were sent outside the territory of the secretariat. If a member of the PJP from your secretariat who had been sent to carry out tasks outside the territory of the secretariat commit a crime or a minor offence, what would the procedure have been?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: Disciplinary procedure would be launched against that member in their -- in the secretariat to which they belonged upon the request of the commander of the unit where he was at the time when he committed that crime or minor offence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you launch disciplinary proceedings in case there was no complaint?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you launch proceedings if you didn't know of a crime committed?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: Well, if we didn't know, we couldn't of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that you have never been informed of the planning and use of the PJP unit that was sent outside your territory?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: On rare occasions we may have known, but mostly they would be sent to a detachment and then they would carry out their mission. Sometimes we would learn of their whereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that in your annual reports you were not able to mention the tasks and activities that your units sent outside your territory were carrying out; rather, you were only in a position to speak about the time-frame and the number of persons sent to such other places and their possible injuries, deaths, and other events?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, because we didn't know what they were doing down there or where they were doing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In simple terms, those units were not under your control?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: When they were outside the territory of the secretariat, they were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right when I say that the chief of the public security department could not suspend or overrule a decision of the minister regarding the deployment of the unit?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: I assume he could not because he was lower in rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could your deputy in Bor suspend any decision of yours?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: No, he could not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Golubovic, reading these statements of yours and the transcript, I came to the conclusion that from 1982 you were an employee of the Ministry of the Interior; am I right?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Before that you worked in the legal affairs department of the mining company Bor and you were a chief also in the SUP of Zajecar?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: First in the SUP of Bor, then the joint secretariat in Zajecar, and then again in the SUP of Bor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe that you were the chief of the SUP with the most years of service in the SUP?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, most probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right, Mr. Golubovic, when I say that on the 6th of April, 1999, when you left and went to Kladovo, you called up the Ministry of the Interior to inform them of the event which you had been informed about and that calling up the ministry you came across the head of the department who was in a MUP building?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can I infer from that that had the head of department not been there you would have informed someone else about the events?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. If I was unable to reach the chief of the department, I would have called one of the other senior officials in the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right that the first reports that you received said that a refrigerator truck had been found in the Danube and that it contained bodies and that these were there as a result of a traffic accident?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: Can I give you a slightly different answer? The first reports were -- referred to a traffic accident without any mention of the victims. And when the refrigerator truck was opened on the 6th, then the reference was to bodies. So on the 5th there was no mention of bodies; it was assumed there were bodies, but we didn't know. And on the 6th it was already known that there were bodies there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did the Kladovo police take all the necessary procedures prescribed by law when the refrigerator truck was found in the Danube?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: According to information I received and reviewing the regulations, I think that they did undertake all the necessary measures. I'm saying this because some of the measures should have been done by the judiciary, by the court, and not the police, so that the police in Kladovo did do everything that was within its terms of reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: That's why I'm saying that the procedures prescribed by law for the police in Kladovo were fulfilled?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right when I say that when informing General Djordjevic you infer -- you concluded that he was surprised and that he heard of this for the first time?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: That is what I said. I think this is in the transcript, that the general was surprised when I informed him of this and that that is perhaps why he said that he would call me back to tell me what to do. So that was my impression based on his reaction. I was not in his presence to be able to see this, but what I could conclude on the basis of our telephone conversation, I think he was surprised.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right when I say that General Djordjevic told you that he would call you back in 15 minutes, and when he did call you he said that he was conveying the instructions of the minister?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: He did call back in 10 or 15 minutes. He didn't say that he was acting on instructions of the minister but he said that the minister said that such and such a thing should be done, he had ordered this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But am I right, Mr. Golubovic, that the order was to implement the procedure in Kladovo, that is, in the territory of the SUP of Bor prescribed by law?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: He didn't give any special order, but the assumption was that the procedure had to be observed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Golubovic, let me ask you, I know that you knew that the investigating judge of the municipal court in Kladovo was present as well as the deputy municipal prosecutor. But were you informed that on the 6th of April, Dr. Trajkovic was also present who was from the medical centre in Kladovo, the coroner, who was there to examine the bodies, and that coffins were brought there too for them to be transported to a certain institute?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, I was told that from the public utility company a certain number of coffins had been loaded on to a truck, but I wasn't told that the doctor was there. I didn't know that. Maybe they omitted to tell me that, so I didn't know that Dr. Trajkovic was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in view of the previous break, can I continue or is it time for the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think we -- are you expecting to be long, Mr. Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, rather longer, but not too long. I think the regular break is at a quarter to 6.00, but we started a little earlier because I asked you to allow me to have that time for preparation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will adjourn now and commence again at ten minutes past 6.00, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I'll speed things up. Thank you. I'll be as quick as I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours -- oh, the witness isn't here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Golubovic, a moment ago we mentioned the investigating judge and the deputy prosecutor. Am I right that the district public prosecutor in Negotin and the investigating judge in Negotin were also informed about the event after the investigating judge of the municipal court and the deputy municipal public prosecutor said that they were not competent for the further procedure?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, I think the municipal prosecutor and the investigating judge informed their counterparts over there, plus the service in Kladovo informed the investigating judge in Negotin.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right when I say that not a single competent prosecutor or investigating judge gave instructions or authorisation for you to carry out an on-site inspection or to carry out further investigative work?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: As far as I'm informed, they refused to take any further measures, I'm referring to the municipal prosecutor and investigating judge, and they stated that they were not competent when they saw the number of bodies in the refrigerator truck and that this was within the competence of the district court.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that your SUP or the units subordinated to you do not have the legal facilities to influence the judicial bodies or the investigating judge or the prosecutors in the municipality or the district to do their work?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: You're right, we cannot instruct them to do something that is not regulated by law.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right when I say that General Djordjevic did not say that the degree of confidentiality should be determined at the level of a state secret?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: You are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right when I say that General Djordjevic was informed about all the steps taken that we have discussed and that he told you just not to make any statements for the media, so as not to avoid further disturbance.

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: When we spoke our conversation went along those lines. It was stated that this information should be kept confidential in view of the state of war, in view of the closeness of the Romanian border, and so that the population should not be further disturbed by this. That was the conversation that we had regarding keeping that information closed, but no one said that it should be a state secret and how could it be when the people of Tekija saw this and they were present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right that this did not apply to the state organs or judicial organs because they were already informed and au courant about the whole thing?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: They were not told even not to broadcast the information; nevertheless, to keep it a state secret.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right if I say that the whole procedure of identification and post mortem investigation would have been done if the number of bodies was 30 that the same procedure would be applied?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: Most probably, though we didn't have the capacity to carry this out in one night. This is a large number. And had the judicial organs taken over their part of the work then it would have been completed there on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right when I say that an on-site inspection was carried out by the investigating judge. Had it been done, then you would have been obliged to follow his instructions regarding the further procedure with the bodies?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: According to the Law on Criminal Proceedings, the investigating judge is in charge of the on-site inspection; and he gives instructions to the police and others what is to be done, whether there would be a post mortem, whether we would just secure the site, and we also secure the evidence, if any; that is what is prescribed by law.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right in saying that in your telephone conversation which you had about 2230 hours with General Djordjevic and when you informed him that you were not able technically to carry out this work nor do you have an institution to do the forensic examinations, that in that conversation General Djordjevic abided by his original instruction that you carry out the procedure?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: I think that when we first discussed this --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: No, I'm talking about your conversation on 11.30 at night. Well, that must have been the first or second conversation from Tekija.

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: No, it is the third, maybe the third overall, but it was the second from Tekija. That is what we discussed, and initially he was in favour of everything being done; but when I explained what the problems were and the difficulties in a subsequent conversation, he agreed; and we acted in accordance with that agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You have moved further. It was only at 2.00 a.m. when you said that work had been stopped and that you were no longer able to continue working, General Djordjevic accepted your initiative for the bodies to be transported to Belgrade or Nis?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Golubovic, you have a great deal of experience as a policeman, and you're also a lawyer. Have you heard in your career of an official note being made without it being signed by the person preparing it?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: It is the practice in the police whoever prepares an official note to sign it, that is customary.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Will you give me a direct answer. Is it possible to make an official note without signing it?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I just want you to be explicit. Let me move on. Even when several persons take part in an action and then an official note is drafted, either the person in charge of that group or another person that he authorises has to sign that official note for the official note to have any legal effect?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that official notes drafted by the SUP or the MUP or the police cannot be used in criminal proceedings as evidence?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. An official note is important for operational work and for investigative bodies before the trial begins under our Law on Criminal Procedure; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct, sir, that it was not established how the refrigerator truck got into the Danube, where it had come from, and who had organised the transport of the bodies?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: That is correct. We had no relevant data, and we couldn't find that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the task force, when they spoke to you, were not interested in the manner of the -- of the truck falling into the Danube?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: I cannot remember all the details, but nobody certainly insisted on that nor was there actually mention of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that you, when you were at Tekija and went to the site of the incident, did not see the truck where the bodies were?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that all these activities took place at night because of the imminent bombing and due to the fact that the site was only a kilometre or less away from the border with Romania and that there were military vessels anchored nearby?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that you told no one that there was an on-site police investigation going on and that the bodies were being photographed?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: That is correct. At a trial, I don't think -- I don't know if it was the Milosevic trial, I said that I didn't forbid anyone to take photographs, and I said that I wasn't at the site itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the -- that staff of the OUP Kladovo conducted all activities on the 6th of April and that you only arrived there around 8.30 or 9.00 p.m. at Kladovo?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And you were in no position to issue orders for the period preceding your arrival?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that with the crime technician Bosko Radojkovic, that you did not have a conversation with him on the 6th and 7th of April?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: I didn't speak to him, but I saw him after the first conversation with the general at his office and when the head of the OUP instructed him what to do with regard to the transportation of the bodies. And maybe he also went to the office because some people did go in there and came out and informed the others who were around to inform us what had been done, that is possible. But we didn't have a conversation really.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the possibility of burying the bodies in a pit, in a nearby pit, was discussed at all?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: When General Djordjevic communicated to us that the minister said that the bodies should be buried, several of us were present at the time, maybe that was -- there was such options put forward, bury them here or there or something like that. Possibly -- it may not have been the chief of the OUP, but possibly somebody else present.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: But that was not really officially considered?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: No, it certainly was not officially considered.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you know that -- of anyone making a suggestion to hand over the truck to the Komunalac public utility company?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: On the following day it was taken to that company, it was towed there, and it stayed there for two or three days. That's the information that I got anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I asked you -- I didn't ask you whether it was taken elsewhere but whether it should be given to Komunalac to be taken possession of it.

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: No, there was some ideas of [indiscernible] going there, et cetera, but that was really out of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Golubovic, as the chief of the SUP at Bor, did you go to briefings at the ministry in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, when there was need, I do think concerning the wartime conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: No, before the war.

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Was it usual practice for chiefs of SUP to go to Belgrade and brief the minister?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, approximately once a month we did have such briefings for the minister or possibly such briefings may have been more frequent in case of extraordinary events. But generally speaking, we had such briefings once a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that you first briefed the minister about the safety and security in the territory of your SUP and that at these meetings that the minister issued you instructions and orders?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: At these briefings what was done first was the heads of administrations to refer about their activities. We followed and then the minister took decisions that were binding on us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And these decisions, were they sent to you in writing after these meetings or briefings with the minister?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: Mostly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you, do you know that in December 1998 the minister adopted a decision about the establishment of a collective body, a council?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: I don't know the details, but I believe there was such a council, and I think it was operational in 1999 and in 2000 also. It wasn't the meeting that I mentioned including us as chiefs of SUPs, but another collective body.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that this -- that the minister had a list of persons who were obliged to come and others who were -- who were invited according to need?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the decision I mentioned envisaged persons in charge of public and state security to be present at the sessions of that council?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: It may have been the case, but I don't know the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: When you're mentioning the minister's meetings with the chiefs of SUPs from all over Serbia, were these meetings attended by people from state security?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: I believe that they were not present, but possibly at one the head of the department of state security was present. I'm not sure, but during that period of a year or two, toward the end. Whether it was in 1998, I'm not sure, but I believe that once the head of that department was present. But otherwise there were only the chiefs of the SUPs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You said that there was such -- one such occasion, but do you know that Mr. Radomir Markovic was assistant minister for criminal police until December 1998?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, I know that, but that's why I'm saying I believe that I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: But then he was assistant for public safety, and later on when he was appointed head of department of state security?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: But that's why I said that people from state security were not present, but I believe that on one occasion -- but I really don't remember because it's been more than ten years, so that on one occasion a representative of state security may have been present, but not more often.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During the war, that is, starting from January 1st, 1999, up until the end of the war, how did these information meetings or briefings in the MUP take place and what did you -- what was the content of the briefing?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: Well, one of the ways to go about it was to hold meetings of that collective council and the other was the -- along the official lines of communication via dispatches. And most times there was the briefings over the phone regarding technical issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: But that was before the war, but your previous question referred to the war period from January of 1999 until the 24th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: But according to the indictment, the wartime conditions were in place starting from the 1st of January, 1999. And what about the period after March 24th?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: After that date, communication was more difficult because all the bodies, including us and the SUPs, moved to other locations, so communication was more difficult. And I believe that it was on the 2nd or 3rd of April that the building of the ministry was bombed, so that communication was much more difficult so that we communicated mostly over the phone or in direct contact when somebody went to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the analyses of administration informed you about current events in Serbia, possibly belatedly, but that no mention was ever made of anti-terrorist activities in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: I cannot remember the details of all that included in all that information, but there was such information -- I mean, information received from the analyses administration. But I cannot give detailed information about the content because it was long ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Okay. If you don't remember, you don't remember. That's all right. I'm interested to hear whether you can tell us anything about the way the minister, Stojiljkovic, ran the ministry. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: I wasn't with the minister often, so I can't really tell. But when he made a decision, he demanded that the decision be implemented, but how he ran the ministry, I really couldn't tell you because I wasn't present there. I know that our chief of the SUP made us carry out his orders without discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me what kind of relationship he had with other high officials in Serbia, what was his political position, if you know?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: Well, that's a question --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: But only if you know; if you don't know, say so freely.

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: I really cannot answer that because I would have to be subjective and possibly say something wrong, so I cannot really assess his behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I only have one more question about the money that was paid. Was it regular procedure to pay people who carried out activities instructed by the MUP?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: It was regular procedure, but the money really was -- was -- it was a small amount. It may have -- in today's terms it would have been about 200 Euros.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Was that anything illegal?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Were they coming for that purpose or to bring the money?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: For that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you give us anything -- give you -- state your opinion about General Djordjevic, even though he's present?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: I've known him since the 1980s when he worked at the SUP in Zajecar and later on I came to the SUP at Bor and later on he left for Belgrade. So from that period in the 1980s, we knew each other. I believe that he held a number of positions because ministers rotated rather often. I believe that he didn't have a high standing with the then-Minister Stojiljkovic. He helped me a lot with my work at the SUP at Bor and he -- we had good official relations. I didn't enjoy special treatment except for the opportunity to have a cup of coffee with him when I went to Belgrade to official meetings. I believe that he carried out his duties in the police in a correct fashion; that's my opinion, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And my last question: As a high police official, did you ever hear or did you ever receive an order to evict Albanian civilians from Kosovo, that they should be terrorised, that their property should be taken away, their houses burnt, that they should be driven out of Kosovo or to tolerate such things?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: No, I never heard of that, and I didn't know of such incidents. Bor was a multi-ethnic municipality, and at the time during the first demonstrations in the 1980s there were -- there were many Albanians at Bor and we -- we, the police, were always ordered to protect their shops, so as to avoid any detrimental consequences. So that's how we functioned at Bor, which was a multi-ethnic town. I can say as much for sure, and I don't know about other areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Golubovic, for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I am done with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djurdjic. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could just take things from the last going back to the beginning of your questioning. You said that Stojiljkovic did not have a high standing -- sorry, you said that the accused, Mr. Djordjevic, did not have a high standing with the minister Stojiljkovic. Can you say how he conducted himself in respect to orders that he might have received from the minister?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: I said that he didn't have a high standing because in those days he held one position then he moved to another, and my impression was that he was not included in all the events, if I can put it that way, and all the agreements reached at that level --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What I'm asking you is this. I'm not asking you for your impressions. I'm just asking you based on your position, did Mr. Djordjevic in his relations with the minister obey his orders or not?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: He acted in accordance with his own competencies. He never issued an order that was not lawful --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That's not what I'm asking you --

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: Now, whether that was in every respect in accordance with the order of the minister, I don't know. I expressed a personal opinion regarding Mr. Djordjevic because I was asked to do so by Defence counsel. That is my personal opinion; it need not necessarily be correct, it is my personal opinion. It's nothing official nor is it proof of anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, that's your impression. You said under the law the investigative judge with jurisdiction over events to be investigated would give instructions as to what needs to be done. In the particular circumstances that you were faced on the 6th of April when a truck had been located with several dozens of dead bodies, would it be normal for the police to ship away the dead bodies without an order to do so from the investigative judge?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: Under normal circumstances, that would most probably not take place; but in view of the circumstances, I don't know what the reasons were that the court did not wish to join in. They refused to do it, so we had no other possibility. We couldn't leave that refrigerator truck with the bodies inside by the road and wait for the court to appear, and we did not have the ability to force them to do that nor could we order them to do that. It was their decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. I'm asking you about transporting the body outside of the municipality. Is that something that you would normally be empowered to do without getting an order from the judge?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: We would do what the court, the investigating judge, tells us to do; that is what the police does, follows instructions from the investigating judge. If he orders a post mortem, they provide a pathologist and we secure the site and we act according to his instructions, especially the prosecutor gives us instructions and we follow them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, in an absence of instructions from the prosecution or the prosecutor or the investigating judge, why did you send the bodies to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: I said that we couldn't keep them there by the road, we couldn't carry it out, the autopsy, the pathological examinations to establish the cause of death, the time of death, et cetera. We didn't have the capacity to do that. I said that in the territory of our SUP we didn't have a single pathologist. The fact that this doctor appeared with the judge, he's not a pathologist. It's necessary for the doctor to be there to simply establish the deaths, but the cause of death is established by a pathologist. And we didn't have the capacity to do this even for 20 men, not to mention the number that we had to do the autopsy and everything else. This is something that takes time, and we would have to bring experts from Belgrade or Nis, Nis was the -- almost the same distance between Nis and Belgrade. So it depended on the capacity of those institutions. So we didn't have any objective possibility to carry this out on the spot. Perhaps if we had some other facilities and if a team were to arrive from the outside we might have done it, but on the ground we were not able to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Having sent the bodies to Belgrade, and in your statement and in your evidence you said you did that on the basis of instructions you got from Mr. Djordjevic. Do you know if any investigations like autopsies were carried out once the bodies arrived in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: I stated in my earlier statements that I didn't know. I simply did the part of the job that was ours. We sent them away, and I didn't inquire any further because I had other things to take care of as the head of the department, and this was no longer the object of my interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. How many times have you had a case in your SUP with 80 bodies, dead bodies, turning up in a truck -- or, scratch the question. I'll move on. You said just now in answer to a question from my friend that initially Mr. Djordjevic was in favour of doing everything, and then you were saying this was probably the second or third time, you weren't sure. What I want to ask you is this: When you first spoke to General Djordjevic, is it -- and that is from the police station in Kladovo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The introduction to the question is an arbitrary construction that is ungrounded, but I do not object to the question. Can the question be put without the introduction when we heard some incorrect interpretations of my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Perhaps you could put your question again, please, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The question is this: You said at one stage initially he was in favour of doing everything. Now, I want to know if by that you mean initially in the course of the second conversation or the first or the third conversation?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC.
utterances.text: As far as I understand the question, though it is not absolutely clear to me, I said that in the first conversation I just informed him what had happened and what I had heard from others. Ten or 15 minutes later the general called and gave instructions that the bodies that were found should be buried in Kladovo because the number was 20 to 30 and that this was the instructions or order because we would usually say the minister ordered when I conveyed a message to someone else I said such and such ordered this. So this was in the first conversation. I didn't quite understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. I think you have answered. I really wanted to ask you about the first conversation what was said, and I think you have answered that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we bring back the rules on the internal organisation of the MUP, and I think that is a document, I'm not sure if it had been given an exhibit number or we were waiting until re-examination, D0020357.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Article 13 thereof, it's on page 9 in the English --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, I'm afraid time is going to beat us. There may be other matters that require attention, but we've reached 7.00 so that we must ask you to continue tomorrow when --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- we proceed. That's unfortunate, but we have run out of time. I would mention that tomorrow because the courtroom in which we were to sit is required for a hearing in the Karadzic case, we will not be able to commence until 3.45. So our commencement will be delayed until 3.45, and when we conclude the evidence of the witness tomorrow, we will need to deal with the question of the documentary exhibit that Mr. Djurdjic wants to tender, the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So I'm sorry then, but we must now adjourn, and we resume tomorrow at 3.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 3rd day of March, 2009, at 3.45 p.m.
